Tech Report: Necessary Losses: The Life-Shaping Art of Letting Go

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “The art of losing isn’t hard to master,” Elizabeth Bishop wrote in one of the great masterpieces of poetry.
  • We dream of immortality because we are creatures made of loss — the death of the individual is what ensured the survival of the species along the evolutionary vector of adaptation — and made for loss: All of our creativity, all of our compulsive productivity, all of our poems and our space telescopes, are but a coping mechanism for our mortality, for the elemental knowledge that we will lose everything and everyone we cherish as we inevitably return our borrowed stardust to the universe.
  • And yet the measure of life, the meaning of it, may be precisely what we make of our losses — how we turn the dust of disappointment and dissolution into clay for creation and self-creation, how we make of loss a reason to love more fully and live more deeply.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The art of losing isn’t hard to master,” Elizabeth Bishop wrote in one of the great masterpieces of poetry. “Every mortal loss is an Immortal Gain,” William Blake wrote two centuries before her in his beautiful letter to a bereaved father.

We dream of immortality because we are creatures made of loss — the death of the individual is what ensured the survival of the species along the evolutionary vector of adaptation — and made for loss: All of our creativity, all of our compulsive productivity, all of our poems and our space telescopes, are but a coping mechanism for our mortality, for the elemental knowledge that we will lose everything and everyone we cherish as we inevitably return our borrowed stardust to the universe.

And yet the measure of life, the meaning of it, may be precisely what we make of our losses — how we turn the dust of disappointment and dissolution into clay for creation and self-creation, how we make of loss a reason to love more fully and live more deeply.

Industry observers note that that is what Judith Viorst explores in her 1987 consolation of a book Necessary Losses (public library) — an inquiry into the profound and far-reaching relationship between our losses and our gains, revealing renunciation as a fulcrum of growth. She paints the vast landscape of loss upon which life plays out:.

Recent findings suggest that when we think of loss we think of the loss, through death, of people we love. But loss is a far more encompassing theme in our life. For we lose not only through death, but also by leaving and being left, by changing and letting go and moving on. And our losses include not only our separations and departures from those we love, but our conscious and unconscious losses of romantic dreams, impossible expectations, illusions of freedom and power, illusions of safety — and the loss of our own younger self, the self that thought it always would be unwrinkled and invulnerable and immortal.

These necessary losses… we confront when we are confronted by the inescapable fact… that we are essentially out here on our own; that we will have to accept — in other people and ourselves — the mingling of love with hate, of the good with the bad;… that there are flaws in every human connection; that our status on this planet is implacably impermanent; and that we are utterly powerless to offer ourselves or those we love protection — protection from danger and pain, from the in-roads of time, from the coming of age, from the coming of death; protection from our necessary losses.

Industry observers note that these losses are a part of life — universal, unavoidable, inexorable. And these losses are necessary because we grow by losing and leaving and letting go.

Sources indicate that as a sculpture is shaped by what is chiseled off from the block of stone, so too are we shaped by what we lose — by choice, with all the complexities and difficulties of letting go, or by the scythe of chance, which takes away as impartially as it gives. Viorst writes:.

According to recent reports, the road to human development is paved with renunciation. Throughout our life we grow by giving up. We give up some of our deepest attachments to others. We give up certain cherished parts of ourselves. We must confront, in the dreams we dream, as well as in our intimate relationships, all that we never will have and never will be. Passionate investment leaves us vulnerable to loss. And sometimes, no matter how clever we are, we must lose… It is only through our losses that we become fully developed human beings.

It has been revealed that we enter the realm of loss the moment the umbilical cord is cut to sever what Viorst calls the “blurred-boundary bliss of mother-child oneness” — the primal loss that sets off the ongoing task of becoming ourselves. From this origin point, she traces the lifelong vector of losses and gains:.

Industry observers note that exchanging the illusion of absolute shelter and absolute safety for the triumphant anxieties of standing alone… we become a moral, responsible, adult self, discovering — within the limitations imposed by necessity — our freedoms and choices. And in giving up our impossible expectations, we become a lovingly connected self, renouncing ideal visions of perfect friendship, marriage, children, family life for the sweet imperfections of all-too-human relationships. And in confronting the many losses that are brought by time and death, we become a mourning and adapting self, finding at every stage — until we draw our final breath — opportunities for creative transformations.

In a sentiment the poet Mark Doty would echo — “you need to both remember where love leads and love anyway,” he wrote in his beautiful reckoning with love and loss — she adds:.

It has been revealed that we cannot deeply love anything without becoming vulnerable to loss. And we cannot become separate people, responsible people, connected people, reflective people without some losing and leaving and letting go.

Complement Necessary Losses, which goes on to explore the many regions of loss in human life and how they can become frontiers of growth, with Hannah Arendt on learning how to live with the fundamental fear of loss, Thoreau on living through a loss, and Alan Watts on learning not to think of gain and loss, then explore two uncommon lenses on loss: fractals and chlorophyll.

#171865. Industry News: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth

Industry News: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern.
  • According to recent reports, in the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades.
  • As the teenagers brainstormed, Jasmin Brooks Stephens, a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth.

According to recent reports, in the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate rose 144% from 2007 to 2020. What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017.

As the teenagers brainstormed, Jasmin Brooks Stephens, a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s Jabali Youth Advocacy organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

“One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she noted, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens intends to translate the results of her study for clinicians and policymakers who are trying to improve suicide prevention for Black youth.

Sources indicate that the ongoing project is just one example of how Brooks Stephens is working to address rising suicide rates among Black youth by engaging them in participatory research—an unusual and hopeful approach in suicide prevention studies. “This summer I had the incredible opportunity to work alongside young people to design a program that would help other young people want to live,” she stated. “Rather than waiting until a young person is already in crisis, I’m interested in understanding what helps youth thrive—what gives them hope and a sense of possibility and helps them recognize the brilliance they have inside them.”.

Despite the growing crisis among Black youth, suicide rates are dropping for adolescents in the U.S. overall. Brooks Stephens finds these statistics revealing: “To me, that suggests that the approaches we have relied on have not adequately addressed the conditions driving suicide risk in Black communities,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that it’s easy to talk about structural racism as an abstract concept, or personal encounters with racists as disturbing but bounded moments. But grappling with racism heavily impacts Black youth and increases their suicide risk, according to a 2023 report from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Indeed, Brooks Stephens has published work documenting how racial discrimination and the COVID-19 pandemic, which disproportionately harmed Black Americans, together worsened suicide risk for Black young adults.

Brooks Stephens’s work is informed by both her research and her own experience of how race can shape young people’s sense of self. “I became aware very early on that Black children are often navigating expectations about who they are supposed to be before they have even had the opportunity to figure out who they are for themselves,” she said. “That has stayed with me—the importance of creating space for Black young people to define themselves, recognize their strengths, and imagine who they want to become.” At the same time, she saw how the stigma surrounding mental health could make it harder for Black youth and families to seek support, even as racism and other chronic stressors were impacting their well-being.

Sources indicate that when she took an African American psychology class as an undergraduate at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, with Enrique Neblett, a renowned scholar of race and health who became her mentor, Brooks Stephens saw the connection between those experiences—and found her passion. “I realized that there was an entire field devoted to understanding how racism affects mental health and how Black children come to understand themselves and their racial identity,” she said.

Later, during her doctoral research at the University of Houston, Brooks Stephens worked with Rheeda Walker, an expert on suicide science and African American adult mental health research. Brooks Stephens noticed that there was very limited discussion about building upstream resilience in suicide prevention research—an approach that focuses on child well-being and happiness before the development of a mental health crisis.

It has been revealed that “We’re studying why people choose to end their life without understanding what makes people want to live,” she said. For Brooks Stephens, that realization opened up a different way of thinking about suicide prevention, one that made room for the strengths that were often absent from traditional models, such as racial identity, spirituality, family connection, belonging, or hope.

It has been revealed that brooks Stephens knows she can’t single-handedly eliminate the racial traumas faced by young Black people. Nor can she end other factors that lead to higher suicide rates in her community, such as systemic injustice or poverty. Instead, she’s focusing on where she can make a difference through her research.

“While I may not be able to eradicate racism, I can help build programs that change how Black young people see themselves and their futures—programs that help them feel grounded in their identity and able to imagine a life that feels worth living,” she noted.

Brooks Stephens and her colleagues identified six positive factors that reduce suicidality among Black youth (courtesy of Jasmin Brooks Stephens).

As a first step, this year she and her colleagues created the Black Youth Thriving Framework for Suicide Prevention. It’s based on a literature review that identified six protective factors that can reduce suicidality among Black youth, including family support, community ties, and self-acceptance. “What we’re working to identify now are the strategies that can help cultivate those strengths in young people’s lives,” Brooks Stephens remarked.

Already, in a study from 2023, she and her colleagues indicated that Black young adults with stronger feelings of self-acceptance are less vulnerable to depression and suicide. Likewise, she has identified mindfulness and meditation as potential tools for Black Americans in their early 20s to buffer the impulsivity that is often associated with suicide risk.

Sources indicate that this approach is a radical departure from the status quo. Right now, resources for preventing suicide orbit around moments of crisis, Brooks Stephens stated. When a child highlights signs of depression or arrives at a hospital following a suicide attempt, that’s when an intervention is often provided. Brooks Stephens wants to develop research-backed ways to prevent a child from ever getting to that troubling point in the first place.

And, increasingly, she is asking Black young people themselves to help determine what those approaches should look like. Brooks Stephens said that the four teens with whom she worked this summer were not simply research participants; they were collaborators in imagining what suicide prevention could become.

Industry observers note that “It’s very uplifting for me because I’m bringing underserved voices into our research and I’m designing solutions,” she noted. “And those solutions are how we make kids want to live and love themselves. That’s it. It’s loving themselves, loving their life. That’s what I’m helping them discover.”.

Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crows can make visual decisions twice as promptly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen.
  • The findings, published in the journal Science, offer latest insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions.
  • Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crows can make visual decisions twice as promptly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

The findings, published in the journal Science, offer latest insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.

Sources indicate that to test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

Recent findings suggest that the birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.".

The results revealed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds.

The team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an key role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

Sources indicate that the recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

Industry observers note that these signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes.

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," indicates Andreas Nieder.

Recent findings suggest that unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as rapidly as primates.

Sources indicate that the researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

Recent findings suggest that however, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

Apex is different — engineering elite racing wheels at an unmatched price point. But when we met them, customers were completely unaware of the difference. In a recent development, we started by naming the problem that Apex solves, calling it The Great Knowledge Void. A state of play where any wheel brand can make performance claims — true or not — just to make a buck. And the worst part? Customers have no way to know the difference. We went on to tell a story of how Apex is fixing this problem with their core ethos: “Real performance.” A pledge to show customers the truth — or die trying. End of story.

Between Psyche and Cyborg: Carl Jung’s Legacy and the Countercultural Courage to Reclaim the Deeply Human in a Posthuman Age

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2356 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “To be a human being among people and to remain one forever, no matter in what circumstances… that’s what life is all about, that’s its task,” the young Dostoyevsky exulted in a letter to his brother just after his death sentence was repealed — death, that great clarifying force for what it means to be alive, what the stakes and sanctities of living are.
  • In the two centuries since, our understanding of what it means to be human, to be mortal and imperfect and ablaze with feeling, has altered dramatically as we have entrusted the cold logic of computation with answering the soul’s cry for connection, for creativity, for meaning — something Dostoyevsky’s contemporary Samuel Butler anticipated in his far-seeing admonition against the dehumanization of humanity in the hands of our machines, something that has metastasized in today’s technocratic cult of posthumanism.
  • In Jung vs Borg: Finding the Deeply Human in a Posthuman Age, Glen Slater bridges ecology, depth psychology, systems theory, and various post-Cartesian philosophies to explore how this civilizational cult has effected “a widening divide between fabrication and authenticity, a loss of more self-aware and soulful modes of living, and an increase in anxiety and depression,” and what we can do to rewild the psyche and reclaim the soul.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“To be a human being among people and to remain one forever, no matter in what circumstances… that’s what life is all about, that’s its task,” the young Dostoyevsky exulted in a letter to his brother just after his death sentence was repealed — death, that great clarifying force for what it means to be alive, what the stakes and sanctities of living are.

In the two centuries since, our understanding of what it means to be human, to be mortal and imperfect and ablaze with feeling, has altered dramatically as we have entrusted the cold logic of computation with answering the soul’s cry for connection, for creativity, for meaning — something Dostoyevsky’s contemporary Samuel Butler anticipated in his far-seeing admonition against the dehumanization of humanity in the hands of our machines, something that has metastasized in today’s technocratic cult of posthumanism.

In Jung vs Borg: Finding the Deeply Human in a Posthuman Age, Glen Slater bridges ecology, depth psychology, systems theory, and various post-Cartesian philosophies to explore how this civilizational cult has effected “a widening divide between fabrication and authenticity, a loss of more self-aware and soulful modes of living, and an increase in anxiety and depression,” and what we can do to rewild the psyche and reclaim the soul.

He begins by drawing an analogy between the catalytic impact of Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring on awakening the modern ecological conscience and the need for a conscious awakening from the dangerous dream of posthumanism into which Silicon Valley has lulled us. Just as the industrial capitalism of Carson’s era commodified our planet’s ecosystems and elemental resources, Slater observes that digital capitalism has “turned our habits of mind into the earth’s most valuable commodity”; just as Carson pioneered the holistic view of ecology that may be our only path to saving Earth, her contemporary Carl Jung pioneered the holistic view of psychology that might, just might, save the human soul from death by commodification.

Whether or not we have turned the ecological corner, there is more consciousness about the way we relate to the world around us and the actions required to avert a climate catastrophe.

Sources indicate that however, the world within us, the inner life of thought and emotion, is another matter. Here integrative understanding has been resisted. The human psyche, the ecosystem of the mind, with its own structures and dynamics, our relation to which is surely as significant as our relation to the outer world, now faces its own significant disruption, one that essentially parallels the syndrome Carson described… The depths of human nature are becoming harder to recognize and protect. Abundant information has furthered scientific knowledge but not human understanding. It has instead left us dazed, confused, and disoriented. Attention, motivation, identity, self-image, and the capacity to reason clearly and imagine deeply are all impacted… While the advantages of digital technologies are impressed upon us at every turn, the rapid entry of these technologies into every aspect of life is evidently impacting our ecology of mind.

With an eye to the urgency of “moving beyond objectification of the earth and of the bodies and minds that inhabit it,” he adds:.

It has been revealed that the technosphere now overlays the ecosphere and we cannot help but inhale its post-industrial gases. Virtuality has begun to displace reality, making the ground of human existence hard to discern… The human psyche and the nature of the whole person are not only suffering in this technospheric environment, the suffering has itself been given over to technological solutions, resulting in a vicious cycle.

The penchant for digital ways of relating, expanding faith in AI, and the one-sided education designed to service these things are combining to generate reductive conceptions of psychological life. We are, in particular, discounting the deeply human… the essential qualities of human experience, which extend from the instinctual patterns that shape basic behavior to the timeless values that mold the cultural imagination. The deeply human anchors the vertical axis of inner understanding; it grounds the ecology of mind. It is also what connects us to the more-than-human. In our era, however, an almost exclusive dedication to a horizontal axis of data gathering threatens this verticality and grounding. This is leading to a world drowning in information and thirsting for understanding.

At the heart of this civilizational crisis is the systemic compartmentalization of our experience, evident in the core polarities and dichotomies of Western culture — past and future, inner and outer, matter and spirit. Pulsating beneath it all is our dissociation from the life of the body, which connects us to the life of the Earth and the life of the universe. Everything beautiful that we touch and see and hear — birdsong, a sunrise, a kiss — is a bittersweet reminder that we have a body and are therefore mortal. Dissociation thrives on the denial of death that began with our ancestors’ mythologies of immortality and is culminating in Silicon Valley’s lurid and lucrative dreams of redesigning human nature, of downloading the mind onto disembodied machines and reducing the soul to a datum.

Pointing to Jung’s timeless cosmogony of the unconscious as the antidote to this damaging delusion, Slater writes:.

Recent findings suggest that jung’s comprehension of the depths of human nature constitutes an incisive counterpoint to the assumptions of posthumanism and to the dissociative bubble that presently fosters these assumptions… Jung sheds light on the self-regulating nature of the psyche and the archetypal forms behind this — forms we may choose to overlook but cannot ultimately dismiss. These forms pertain to brain structure, anatomy, and evolved patterns of perception and behavior. But they also reflect the larger rhythms of the cosmos and are seemingly woven into the fabric of life itself. Jung pointedly demonstrates that even as we have embraced reason and science, the archetypal world of non-rational impulses and religious ideas have continued to unconsciously influence our thoughts and actions.

Jung’s crowning contribution was to invite an understanding of the psyche as the foundation of all perception, experience, thought, feeling, and action — the wellspring of our humanity. In exploring the psychology of the unconscious with all of its interlaced convolutions — archetypes and complexes, projections and introjections — Jung illuminated the way our dreams and fantasies unconsciously shape the course of our lives, the way our arts and sciences cohere into a vast collective unconscious that shapes the course of our civilization. With an eye to Jung’s legacy, Slater writes:.

It has been revealed that it is the psyche that contains the pursuit of the angelic, the claims of the animal body, and the structures and dynamics that join the two. It is the psyche that generates and insists upon the symbolic expressions of culture, which are often based on the transformative and aspirational power of ordinary, even elemental, things — mountains and rivers, suns and moons, fire and rain — thereby reminding us of the inextricable bond between mind and world. If cosmic matter has given rise to consciousness, and we are now called to grasp the nature of consciousness, realizing that thinking about our thinking is the necessary companion of any exploration and understanding of the universe that surrounds us, our grasp of the inner world becomes just as vital as our grasp on the outer world — perhaps even more so.

Nearly a century after the Swiss poet, philosopher, and linguist Jean Gebser made his exquisite case for the evolution of consciousness, Slater reflects on Jung’s legacy and writes:.

According to recent reports, godlike power necessitates godlike responsibility. This begins with self-awareness, which is rooted in a sober consideration of the human psyche, the most critical part of which is shedding light on the shadow side of our willful pursuits… Will and reason alone cannot form a seat of wise agency — a far more expansive consciousness is required.

Industry observers note that an expansion of consciousness is imperative if we are to make responsible use of the transformative power in our hands… With divine guidance largely beyond our secular vision, we are left to look within for something deeper than our controlling inclinations and to look without to perceive the guidance of nature’s intelligence. Guidance must ultimately come from dialogue with these marginalized sources of knowledge and from the cultural imagination, which shapes this dialogue. The result will be a “co-creation” — a partnership between innovation, self-knowledge, and a cosmology befitting this age. Such a co-creative process will mitigate and shape our technologies as well as generate opportunities for spiritual renewal.

Such co-creation, Slater argues, demands a reanimated view of existence — one that “counters the commodification of all things that is currently consuming us,” one that “conveys a confluence of spirit and matter — the very means by which a sense of soul is generated.” He writes:.

According to recent reports, A reanimated world is one in which spirit and matter are not just equally regarded but recognized as mutually dependent. The great task of this late modern era is thus to bring together what the spiritual preoccupations of the old world and the material focus of the latest world have torn apart. The psyche reveals us this dependency whenever a person or group attempts to embrace one without the other, in the way the neglected side begins to rule the unconscious… But the earth process itself suggests we rediscover nature as spirit as well as understand it as matter — nature as presence, intelligence, and root source of inspiration and imagination… Both mind and earth are calling for perspectives capable of marrying these dimensions of reality.

Countering this fragmentation of reality requires, above all, learning to resist our dissociative tendencies and trust our emotions — for, as philosopher Martha Nussbaum observes in her masterwork on the intelligence of the emotions, “emotions are not just the fuel that powers the psychological mechanism of a reasoning creature, they are parts, highly complex and messy parts, of this creature’s reasoning itself.” Slater considers the building blocks of this self-trust:.

Such trust begins with a natural appreciation of emotional intelligence and the guiding potential of this intelligence, which can feel like it emanates from a will of its own. This trust may grow over a long time or it may come as a sudden life-lesson. But few things beyond the contemplation of emotional responses open the door to the deeply human and the awareness of having an inner partner [that] operates apart from conscious, rational direction. To be full of emotion is to be animated by something in spite of ourselves; perhaps this is why we end up regularly conversing with the sadness or anger that grips us. Emotions like these stand in need of negotiation, mollification or perhaps just more attention. Often, when we want to keep moving on, the emotions will not allow it. And sometimes when we would choose to hold back, emotions charge ahead.

Because our emotions are a fundament of our human nature, which is itself a fractal of Nature, they are the raw material for the co-creative process that offers an antidote to the dehumanization of humanity. Slater writes:.

We are affected by desire for more satisfying ways of being, outrage about all that is regularly exploited and destroyed, fear of what stresses and overwhelms, and shame about participating in the machinations of it all. To consider the way emotion comes upon us, from a nature we call “ours,” all the while being a branch of Nature itself, calls into question whether these emotions even belong to us or to the sufferings of the world, and we are being directed to feel and respond on its behalf. In other words, our animation may be the world’s way of speaking to us, and thus be an indispensable dimension of the co-creative process. Recognition of the autonomous intelligence of these deep emotional responses may be an invitation to attune ourselves to the presence of the earth’s own intelligence — or intelligences.

It is the psyche that bridges these regions of intelligence, the inner and the outer, the human and the cosmic, death and life. Slater writes:.

The psyche, which is obviously grounded in nature, also leads us beyond this ground, into a concern with destiny and leaving some trace of ourselves in service to humanity… We neither have to lean on notions of a spirit that literally departs the body, nor on fantasies of downloading our minds. Rather, we accept that the substance of psychic experience, accumulated over a lifetime, marks everything we do and everyone around us. And such a marking can be dreamed on. Life and death thus intertwine to produce defining qualities of being.

In a passage evocative of James Baldwin’s soulful insistence that “it is necessary… to know that in oneself, waiting to be found, there is a light,” and that “everything in our lives depends on how we bear the light,” Slater adds:.

In a recent development, the wonder of psychological life is that this dimming of the ego-light allows the perception of another light, one that has been in the background all along… Posthumanism brightens the ego-light, the light of the intellect and will that blankets the light of natural consciousness the wise ape presents to us. It fails to reconcile our spiritual reach and our instinctual ground. It cracks cultural vessels that have always incubated this reconciliation and truncates rather than extends the human experiment.

Lensing Jung’s legacy through the light of thinkers as varied as Hannah Arendt, William James, Yuval Harari, and Oliver Sacks, Slater goes on to explore and celebrate the countercultural movement in the margins of this techno-trance — ways of seeing and of being that, unlike posthumanism, refuse to exclude beauty, eros, and transcendence from the human story, a story told in the language of the soul, irreducible to data. Complement Jung vs Borg with Iain McGilchrist on how we render reality, James Bridle on rethinking intelligence, and Pierre Teilhard de Chardin on bridging the scientific and the sacred, then revisit Jung himself on the most key paradigm for living.

What Happens When Elders Share Their Stories

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community.
  • Recent findings suggest that the local historical society took interest in this idea, which led to an exhibit at the 159-year-old Tunbridge World’s Fair, and a book series entitled Folk Life: Tunbridge Oral Histories.
  • According to recent reports, what is it about life stories that strikes such a universal chord?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community. Knowing there was a significant senior population here, I reached out to the town librarian with hopes of helping elders share their stories.

Recent findings suggest that the local historical society took interest in this idea, which led to an exhibit at the 159-year-old Tunbridge World’s Fair, and a book series entitled Folk Life: Tunbridge Oral Histories. The first two print runs sold out. The second collection of stories has just been published, and people are already asking who will be featured in the third.

According to recent reports, what is it about life stories that strikes such a universal chord? And why is it important—and even imperative—to share our stories with others? I interviewed oral historians, teachers, and a digital storyteller to discover more about why the age-old tradition of recording oral histories continues to make such a significant impact for individuals and communities.

Industry observers note that storytelling is, according to scientific research, a biological shortcut to human connection. Uri Hasson and fellow researchers at Princeton University discovered that the brains of the storyteller and listener physically sync up while a story is being told, promoting social connection, trust, and empathy.

In a recent development, the more emotionally affecting the story is, the stronger this connection becomes. As emotions and tension rise, hormones are released, including oxytocin, the “bonding hormone”; dopamine, which sharpens focus; and cortisol, which promotes attention and alertness as conflicts in the story arise. These hormonal responses enhance both the listener’s memory and connection to the storyteller.

For Erin Barnaby, a digital storyteller and 11th-generation Tunbridge native, oral histories create a connection not only to people, but also time and place. “My dad recently sold his house to my uncle, a house that he built on land that my grandfather had given to him. I love to hear him tell stories about the shifting of the land, from sheep farms to dairy farms and the shift from open pastures to forests.”.

Industry observers note that even when the subject matter might not be instantly relatable, the process of listening to another’s stories still creates a profound interpersonal connection. Esther Ehrlich, who worked at UC Berkeley’s Oral History Center for six years before launching an oral history business of her own, experienced this sense of connection firsthand:.

Sources indicate that I was assigned an interview with a former medical malpractice insurance guy, which initially didn’t interest me at all. And then lo and behold, after interviewing this man, I found him absolutely fascinating. What I came to discover was that by the time we were done, or even partway in, I came to love every single person I interviewed. I would feel connected to them and them to me.

From that biological and psychological basis, oral histories make a critical social contribution.

According to the Oral History Association, “oral history is the oldest type of historical inquiry, stemming from the oral traditions of myriad cultures across the globe, predating even the written word.” These personal stories expand upon the narratives of history books, allowing people from varied walks of life to share their unfiltered experiences and perspectives. Indeed, many works by trained historians rely on oral histories.

The founders of Voice of Witness, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing human rights by amplifying unheard voices, believe that oral history “can democratize history, contribute to narrative change, and illuminate issues and events in a profoundly powerful way.” Enabling individuals to safely share their stories opens people’s minds to fresh perspectives and vantage points.

It has been revealed that while oral histories are limited to an individuals’ memories and are by nature subjective, they remain incredibly valuable in their ability to paint a portrait of time and place. Plus, their narrative-driven format brings history to life in a more memorable way than date- and fact-focused textbooks.

Helen Marks, a former history teacher who has spoken to thousands of students about her experience as a hidden child in Belgium during World War II, has observed that when a person shares their stories, it brings that part of history to life:.

I am among the few surviving hidden children who are willing and able to talk about their experiences in the Holocaust. Reading numbers on a page does not create the same impact as someone standing or sitting in front of you describing a moment that was frightening or was so foreign they didn’t know what to do. . . . I think that when you connect a face, no matter what the face looks like, you get a wholly different reaction than when you read a page full of facts.

Throughout the interviews I conducted for Folk Life, the importance of leaving a meaningful legacy was a common theme. “That’s the reason we share our stories,” says Marsha Higgins, a history teacher for nearly 40 years. “It makes us feel like we matter.”.

Higgins taught students to create personal narratives from a young age. Decades later, former students still express their thanks for her guidance in teaching them the importance of recording their experiences.

“I encouraged students to write down things that happened to them. It’s helpful to know at the time, you’re creating chapters in your life, that your story is just as interesting as anybody else’s.”.

Like Marks, Higgins grew up around immigrants from Europe. “And they all had stories,” she says. “Whenever we got together, somebody would tell me a story. How do you make conversation without one? It’s just so much a part of who we are.”.

“I think everyone wants to know that they have made a positive difference,” says Marks. “That they did some good, that their being here wasn’t just a fleeting moment of nothingness, but that they contributed something. They reacted to something. They gave something. So when you tell stories, that’s where you learn about people and what they value.”.

Neal Allen, a coach and author (most recently of Good Writing: 36 Ways to Improve Your Sentences with his wife Anne Lamott), spent several years as a hospice volunteer. During that time, he helped a number of people share and record their stories.

Recent findings suggest that “Every week I had one or two clients who were dying, and I spent time fluffing their pillows, listening to their stories and how they approach death. The funny thing is we were always asked, ‘Oh, isn’t that hard?’ It was quite the opposite. It was really quite extraordinary.”.

A seasoned journalist, Allen knew how to ask evocative questions. “Oddball memories were coming up that hadn’t come up in 50 years maybe,” he claims, which led to more and more stories. “My subjects would get really involved in it. To finish their story, it would take eight to 12 hours, sometimes up to 40 hours.”.

Allen wrote a biography about his father, which proved to be a learning opportunity for both him and his brothers:.

Once [the book] was bound and we read it all the way through, we had the same reaction, ‘Oh, I didn’t know he had done this. Oh, I didn’t know he had done this. Oh, did you know about that?’ Our second reaction was, ‘We’re not in it,’ and burst out laughing. It was easy to laugh about because he never, ever gave us any sign that he disapproved of us in any fundamental way.

For older adults, sharing stories not only connects them with family, each other, and audiences, it also exercises the brain and fosters a sense of well-being. Story sharing activates memory networks while encouraging reflection on past experiences.

Reminiscence therapy, a structured method of helping individuals recall, organize, and share life stories, has proven helpful in elevating people’s moods, enhancing their self-esteem, resolving conflict, and promoting meaning. This mode of therapy is becoming increasingly popular as a way to support seniors facing cognitive decline as well as mental health challenges.

Ehrlich notes that more than ever, hearing or reading about others’ stories is a powerful tool for building bridges, especially in this divisive climate.

“We have so much more in common than not,” she notes, noting that “there’s a desperate need to understand each other better. Oral history is perhaps a tool for seeing beyond our rigid ideas of who people are and breaking through into a fuller understanding.”.

It has been revealed that “What always astonished the subject of the memoirs was how many people they had touched,” notes Allen. “I think we touch a far greater number of people than we can hold or remember at any one time.”.

In this way, sharing stories reminds us that our interactions have more of an impact than we realize, not only in our close-knit circles, but also at work, at school, and even in everyday exchanges.

What sharing our stories boils down to, Ehrlich believes, is that it’s a fundamental human instinct:.

Recent findings suggest that how do we live a life? How do we deal with joy and difficulty and disappointment and pleasure? How do we make choices? What do we have control over? What don’t we have control over? Oral histories, at their most basic, include all the stuff that makes us people, including our desire to be seen, heard, and understood. And everybody’s stories matter.

In a recent development, elisse Gabriel is a senior writer and editor, with clients ranging from schools, museums, and nonprofits to national retailers, tech startups, and Fortune 500 companies. Currently, she is working on a middle grade novel that celebrates the superpower of sensitivity in boys.

Where the Joy Is

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the most key things I have learned about life is that joy is a choice, an orientation, a practice of bending the mind in the direction of gladness — a choice increasingly countercultural in our age of competitive complaint, and yet all the more urgent precisely because our world gives us so many valid reasons for despair.
  • Joy is not difficult to find, but it can be difficult to trust — partly because the merchants of pseudo-morality have sold us the dangerous myth that, in an unjust world, despair is an emblem of our solidarity with justice, and partly because in this age of grandiosity, we have forgotten that joy is a plurality of smallnesses: a function of what Hermann Hesse called “the little joys” that light up a life with presence.
  • It has been revealed that we need them, these reminders that joy is not a denial of suffering but the fulcrum of our resilience in its midst; that it comes to us not with horns and cymbals but as a distant whisper from the birthplace of the ordinary, not like a bouquet of roses offered with champagne but like the lovely little weed blooming through a crack in the sidewalk of the quotidian.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most key things I have learned about life is that joy is a choice, an orientation, a practice of bending the mind in the direction of gladness — a choice increasingly countercultural in our age of competitive complaint, and yet all the more urgent precisely because our world gives us so many valid reasons for despair. “Experience of conflict and a load of suffering has taught me that what matters above all is to celebrate joy… Life is wasted when we make it more terrifying, precisely because it is so easy to do so,” the artist René Magritte wrote in his timeless manifesto for the courage of joy in the wake of the second World War of his life. “We’ve all had too much sorrow — now is the time for joy,” Nick Cave sang an epoch later as he contemplated the paradox of joy against the backdrop of unimaginable loss.

Joy is not difficult to find, but it can be difficult to trust — partly because the merchants of pseudo-morality have sold us the dangerous myth that, in an unjust world, despair is an emblem of our solidarity with justice, and partly because in this age of grandiosity, we have forgotten that joy is a plurality of smallnesses: a function of what Hermann Hesse called “the little joys” that light up a life with presence.

It has been revealed that we need them, these reminders that joy is not a denial of suffering but the fulcrum of our resilience in its midst; that it comes to us not with horns and cymbals but as a distant whisper from the birthplace of the ordinary, not like a bouquet of roses offered with champagne but like the lovely little weed blooming through a crack in the sidewalk of the quotidian. And that is precisely what artist-philosopher Maira Kalman offers in her book Joy (public library) — a love letter to the sweet strangeness of life, to its unboastful wonderland of small miracles, to the way it expands and expands and expands the moment we contract the aperture of attention onto a single unit of gladness.

that suffering and sorrow envelop our planet and our little lives.

And then it goes where we, short-termists of the present, rarely go: into the lives of some of her heroes who lived through times and turmoils far more unimaginable than ours: She paints Alfred Dreyfus sitting in his prison cell on Devil’s Island; she paints the bedroom in which Beethoven, fully deaf, wrote “Ode to Joy”; she paints Virginia Woolf and her “surprisingly colorful” sitting room just before she filled her coat pockets with stones and waded into the River Ouse; she paints Kafka under the black hat he wore as a helmet of despair, his hand rested tenderly on his beloved dog.

As if to remind us that we are always in relationship with those whose lives have touched ours, whether living or dead, whether or not we have ever met them, she paints her imaginary conversations with Gertrude Stein, with James Baldwin, with Vladimir Nabokov.

Dog punctuate this love letter to joy, cradled in arms and curled in corners, peeking from the pages with their searching eyes and their uncomplicated sweetness: “Isn’t that the answer to everything,” she writes with an eye to a friend who tends to her four dogs “with unlimited care and love.”.

And people, of course, so many people with their strange and soulful faces, each a universe of feeling conjured up with just a few brush strokes.

What might happen if you could leave gloom (pervasive) and perils (lurking) for just a little bit?

What solace might you find if you turned your gaze to a thing of beauty.

She reverences trees, “kind and strong and loving,” and a medieval painting of “a saint with a terrific hairdo” at the Met, and a beautiful man with a porkpie hat at the bookstore, and the fig tree in a friend’s backyard, and people singing, and a young man playing Bach on his violin under the cherry tree, and Pablo Casals playing Bach on his cello while smoking a pipe.

And isn’t it true we are lost without music?

Do children not give us our reason?

Page by page of these small reveries — birdsong, a summer breeze, books and libraries, a woman “lost in thought basking in the morning sun with her little dog by her side,” the bowl of fresh berries on a dying friend’s table, the way a garden, any garden, “can fill you with elation,” the way sitting by the ocean, any ocean, is “enough to make your spirits soar,” the way holding a child’s gaze can make you “forget all the sorrows of the world” — you discover that any moment of joy contains “the essence of what it means to be alive.”.

And don’t I know, and don’t you know, how one sublime instant, one sublime, fleeting instant, changes everything and makes the world right?

It isn’t nothing, that instant — this atom of time, this unit of eternity, the only thing we ever have that is ours for the keeping. “Time is a reality confined to the instant and suspended between two voids,” philosopher Gaston Bachelard wrote. Because attention is what fills the instant with reality, how we spend our attention is how we spend our lives. Emerging from these painted pages is a beckoning to train our attention on joy in all its variousness, its unassuming abundance, its sacred smallness.

Breaking: Lotus L. Kang wins Canada’s top art prize, the Sobey Art Award

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) and the Sobey Art Foundation named the artist Lotus L.
  • The other five shortlisted artists—Melaw Nakehk'o (from the Circumpolar region), Samuel Roy-Bois (Pacific), Audie Murray (Prairies), Caroline Monnet (Québec) and Shane Perley-Dutcher (Atlantic)—will each receive C$25,000 ($17,500), while the 24 longlisted artists each received C$10,000 ($7,000), bringing the total value of the award to C$465,000 ($325,800).
  • According to recent reports, in a statement, Jonathan Shaughnessy, the chair of the jury for this year’s Sobey Art Award, praised Kang for “the commitment and rigour demonstrated in her practice for well over a decade”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) and the Sobey Art Foundation named the artist Lotus L. Kang asthe winner of the 2026 Sobey Art Award during a ceremony on Saturday (14 November). The Toronto-born, New York-based photographer, sculptor and installation artist won the 23rd edition of the annual award, the most high-profile and lucrative prize devoted to Canadian contemporary artists, and will receive C$100,000 ($70,000).

The other five shortlisted artists—Melaw Nakehk'o (from the Circumpolar region), Samuel Roy-Bois (Pacific), Audie Murray (Prairies), Caroline Monnet (Québec) and Shane Perley-Dutcher (Atlantic)—will each receive C$25,000 ($17,500), while the 24 longlisted artists each received C$10,000 ($7,000), bringing the total value of the award to C$465,000 ($325,800).

According to recent reports, in a statement, Jonathan Shaughnessy, the chair of the jury for this year’s Sobey Art Award, praised Kang for “the commitment and rigour demonstrated in her practice for well over a decade”. He continued: “Through installations using unfixed photographic film, cast and found objects, and fabricated armatures, her practice resists the stabilising impulses traditionally associated with photography. Reoccurring motifs including lotus root, flowers, soju bottles, birds, anchovies, are not fixed objects, but repositories of place, longing and desire.”.

It has been revealed that partial view of Lotus L. Kang's installation In Cascades (2023-24) in Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing at the Whitney Museum of American Art Photo: The Art Newspaper.

Kang, a recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2024 whose work was included in the 2024 Whitney Biennial and the 2025 Shanghai Biennale, works across sculpture, photography and site-responsive installation. Her materially dense, non-linear installations explore the liminal space between industrial and architectural forms, familial and social histories, as well as poetry and non-human figures. One of her celebrated installation works, Mother (2020), comprised dozens of metal mixing bowls filled with scattered abstract clay, rubber and stone sculptures as well as aluminium casts of fruit and anchovies. Her critically acclaimed solo exhibition at 52 Walker in Newly introduced York last year featured several greenhouse installations as well as one made of strips of film extended around a spinning rotary dryer.

According to recent reports, “It is an honour to be recognised by this prize,” Kang noted in a statement. “I am grateful to those I love, those who love me and those who have supported me; you keep me going. The recognition of this prize means that askew ideas are worth pursuing. Art is essential to life, progress and love.”.

During the ceremony, Kang told those assembled at the NGC and those watching via livestream: “I just want to congratulate the other artists. It’s an honour to be nominated alongside you. Shane, Melaw, Caroline, Audie, Samuel. It is really inspiring to be showing alongside you, and who knows what would have happened, and I’m just glad we’ll all keep making art, because it’s really the best thing. So, thank you so much.’’.

Lotus L. Kang, Receiver Transmitter (49 Echoes I), 2022-25 © Lotus Kang. Photo: Courtesy of the artist and 52 Walker gallery, Fresh York.

According to recent reports, rob Sobey, the chair of the Sobey Art Foundation, offered his “heartfelt congratulations” to Kang and added: “We also celebrate tonight all 29 artists on this year’s longlist and shortlist for their creativity and vision. We are proud to champion their work and grateful to the National Gallery of Canada for helping bring these remarkable artistic voices to audiences at home and around the world.”.

Selected by an independent jury of curators and cultural leaders, Kang was chosen following a rigorous review process. The jury, who evaluated the artists’ practices, achievements, and contributions to contemporary art in Canada included Kimberly Phillips, the director of the Marianne and Edward Gibson Art Museum at Simon Fraser University, representing the Pacific region;Daisy Desrosiers, a curator at large for North America at Tate, representing the Quebec region;and Helen Nisbet, the director of Glasgow International, serving as international juror.

Works by all six shortlisted artists are right now featured in the 2026 Sobey Art Award Exhibition at the NGC in Ottawa (until 3 January 2027).

Industry observers note that the late Frank H. Sobey, an enthusiastic collector of Canadian art, established the Sobey Art Foundation in 1981 and the Sobey Art Award was launched in 2002. Five years ago, the award’s criteria were amended from a prize devoted to “emerging artists” under 40 to recognising artists of any age who are at a “critical juncture” in their careers. Past winners have included Brian Jungen (in 2002), Annie Pootoogook (2006), Abbas Akhavan (2015), Laakkuluk Williamson Bathory (2021) and Nico Williams (2024).
